sweep_summary: Norwegian (norw1258) is in the catalog as weight-hedged (weight-sensitive (tentative), right-edge three-syllable window; deciding source Rice 2006 / ROA-747). I re-downloaded ROA-747 and verified the catalog quote at pp.1-2 and p.7. All five title-works with stress in the title are about tonal accent (Accent 1/2) or Old Norwegian syntax, none about stress placement: Tiemann 2022 (Old Norwegian OV/VO, constituent weight; abstract read via Crossref, irrelevant); Withgott & Halvorsen 1988 (paywalled de Gruyter / restricted archive.org lending copy; tonal accent representation, low priority); Kelly & Smiljanić 2017 (Karger paywalled; abstract read, Trøndersk tonal accent acoustics, silent on stress); Wetterlin 2010 (paywalled, but its open 2006 Konstanz thesis was downloaded and read — it presupposes stress and explicitly declines to state Standard East Norwegian stress rules); Morén 2005 (abstract recovered from the Internet Archive copy of the 13mfm booklet, scanned of an image page — boundary-tone analysis of stød/pitch accent, silent on stress placement). The best first-hand stress statement read is Lunden 2006 (ROA-833, held by the project from the earlier reading): final stress on consonant-final words, else penult, else antepenult when penult light and antepenult heavy, with listed minor patterns — confirms and refines the catalog's classification without superseding Rice 2006. Still unread and worth acquiring for completeness (not for the classification): Kristoffersen 2000 The Phonology of Norwegian chs. 6-7 (OUP, paywalled) and Lunden 2013 JCGL (paywalled), both already noted; all lookups were done by direct downloads (ROA, KOPS, Crossref, Europe PMC, Karger, the Internet Archive/CDX).

new_statements.quote: I claim that stress falls on the final syllable when possible. The final syllable may bear stress if it is underlyingly /CVC/ or /CVCC/. (In the former instance it will be augmented to CV:C.) Stress is otherwise penultimate, a light /CV/ being augmented to CV:. The quantity sensitive nature of the language can be seen in words that have the shape /CVC.CV.CV/. In such cases the antepenult, rather than the penult, will be stressed, as it is underlyingly heavy. Thus, we may state the basic stress pattern as in (28). (28) a. If the word ends in a consonant, stress the final syllable b. Otherwise, stress the penult c. Unless the penult is light and the antepenult is heavy, in which case, stress the antepenult

new_statements.reading: A first-hand, lexicon-based (Kristoffersen's loanword database, checked with a native speaker) plus novel-word-experiment statement of Norwegian primary-stress placement: right-edge, quantity-sensitive three-syllable window — final stress on consonant-final (closed) finals, otherwise penult, antepenult only when the penult is light and the antepenult heavy; native words (mono- or CVX.C-disyllabic) have invariant initial stress; predictable minor patterns ([s]-, [Cs]-, [er]/[et]-final words take penult; final-hiatus V-final words take antepenult) and a residue of true exceptions (French/Greek vowel-final loans with final stress, bison). Lunden adds (p.108) that the pattern 'is thought to be consistent across dialects of Norwegian'. This CONFIRMS and REFINES the catalog's weight-hedged / weight-sensitive (tentative) coding built on Rice 2006 (right-edge alignment, NonFinality overridden by bimoraic finals, weight partly lexical): same window, same weight logic, with the exception classes spelled out. It does not contradict anything in the Rice quote.

tone_statements.citation: Bye, Patrik (2025). Lexical accent and intonation in Peninsular North Germanic: pragmatics, phonology, geography, history. In Pavel Iosad & Björn Köhnlein (eds), Synchronic and Diachronic Approaches to Tonal Accent (Oxford Studies in Phonology and Phonetics), 146-174. Oxford: Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/9780191988080.003.0006.
tone_statements.quote: Lexical ‘accent 2’ in Peninsular North Germanic may be realized with one or two peaks, depending on the dialect, raising the question which type has diachronic priority. While Riad (1998b, et seq.) makes the case for a two-peaked origin, the chapter presents a one-peaked origin theory, arguing that Gårding and Lindblad’s (1973) types are related in the diachronic sequence 1A > 1B > 2A > 2B. Building on Hognestad (2012), the most important phonetic driver of this change is identified as the Effort Code (Gussenhoven 2004).
tone_statements.summary: Dialect typology of the Scandinavian lexical accent 2 (one- vs two-peaked) with a diachronic derivation of the Norwegian/Swedish accent types.

tone_statements.citation: Solhaug, Tor Håvard (2024). Tone and internal word structure: The interface between morphosyntax and phonology in a variety of Northern Norwegian. PhD dissertation, UiT The Arctic University of Norway (supervisor A. Fábregas). hdl:10037/33755. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: Tromsø Norwegian is a variety of Norwegian that is part of the mainland Scandinavian isogloss in which a contrast between two tonal accents, known as accent 1 and accent 2, has developed. The distribution of the two tonal accents in morphologically complex words is subject to both phonological and morphosyntactic factors, which interact in non-trivial ways. ... this dissertation sides with research that only allows lexical marking of accent 1, whereas accent 2 is always post-lexical and thus belongs to phonology proper.
tone_statements.summary: Two tonal accents (accent 1 lexically marked, accent 2 default/post-lexical) in Tromsø Norwegian; accent assignment in compounds conditioned by morphosyntax.

tone_statements.citation: Kristoffersen, Gjert (2018). Tonelagsspredning på Strilelandet. Maal og Minne 2018(2): 29-81. hdl:11250/3396593. [Companion: Kristoffersen, G. (2016). Fravær av tonelag på Strilelandet: en forskningshistorie. Maal og Minne 2016(2): 111-157, hdl:11250/3350785.]
tone_statements.quote: Denne artikkelen beskriver og analyserer hvordan tonelagskontrasten sprer seg fra bergensmålet til bygdemålene rundt byen, de såkalte strilemålene. Disse har så langt tilbake vi har kilder, ikke hatt tonelagskontrast, men dette er nå raskt i ferd med å endre seg. ... Mønsteret som avtegner seg, er at den bergenske tonelagskontrasten i form av en tidlig tonetopp i tonelag 1 mot en markert senere i tonelag 2, fonetisk sett gradvis vinner terreng.
tone_statements.translation: This article describes and analyses how the tonal accent contrast is spreading from the Bergen dialect to the rural dialects around the city, the so-called Stril dialects. As far back as we have sources these have not had a tonal accent contrast, but this is now rapidly changing. ... The emerging pattern is that the Bergen accent contrast, an early tonal peak in accent 1 versus a markedly later one in accent 2, is gradually gaining ground phonetically.
tone_statements.summary: Stril (rural Bergen-area) Norwegian traditionally lacks the accent 1/2 contrast; younger speakers adopt the Bergen system (accent 1 early H peak, accent 2 late peak).

tone_statements.citation: Kelly, Niamh Eileen (2015). An Experimental Approach to the Production and Perception of Norwegian Tonal Accent. PhD dissertation, The University of Texas at Austin (supervisor Rajka Smiljanić). doi:10.15781/T29W2K; hdl:2152/31494.
tone_statements.quote: This dissertation examines the lexical tonal accent contrast of the Trondersk dialect of East Norwegian from the perspective of both production and perception. ... The Trondersk dialect is unusual typologically in that it exhibits a tonal contrast on monosyllabic words. ... The results of the acoustic analysis revealed that the main correlate of the disyllabic accent distinction in this dialect was in the timing of the F₀ contour, with accent 2 having a later alignment of F₀ landmarks and a higher F₀ minimum than accent 1.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tonal accent (accent 1 vs accent 2) in Trøndersk, contrastive even on monosyllables (circumflex), realized as HL contours differing in F0 timing; enhanced under contrastive focus.

tone_statements.citation: Hognestad, Jan Kristian (2012). Tonelagsvariasjon i norsk: synkrone og diakrone aspekter, med særlig fokus på vestnorsk. Doctoral dissertations at the University of Agder 40. Kristiansand: Universitetet i Agder. 282 pp. ISBN 978-82-7117-701-0.
tone_statements.quote: Nevertheless, in any Norwegian dialect displaying the tonal accent contrast, all words of more than one syllable are pronounced with one of the two accentual melodies. … High tone dialects are characterized by a H tone (the focus tone mentioned above) on the main stress syllable in Accent 1 words, followed by a boundary L. Low tone dialects have a L tone in the main stress position, whereas the focal H, which also doubles as a boundary tone, occurs at the far right end of the accentual domain. This LH contour is the standard situation in Eastern Norwegian dialects.
tone_statements.locator: English Summary, pp. 259-260; cf. ch. I sec. 3.1-3.2 pr. pp. 8-10 and ch. V sec. 3.1 pr. p. 156
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tonal accents (tonelag 1, tonelag 2) on every polysyllabic word, analysed as H/L melodies anchored at the stressed syllable (West HL vs LHL, East LH vs HLH); plus primary word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Kristoffersen, Gjert (2006). Is 1 always less than 2 in Norwegian tonal accents? In Michiel de Vaan (ed.), Germanic Tone Accents: Proceedings of the First International Workshop on Franconian Tone Accents, Leiden 2003 (Zeitschrift für Dialektologie und Linguistik, Beihefte 131), 63-71. Stuttgart: Franz Steiner. Open postprint: Bergen Open Research Archive hdl:1956/2419.
tone_statements.quote: As in Swedish, a tonal accent distinction is found in most Norwegian dialects. The distinction is dependent on primary stress, so that any primary stress will be pronounced with one of the two melodies that manifest the accent distinction. The phonetic manifestation of the melodies will vary with dialect, but two main groups can be identified. The East Norwegian type ... Here, accent 1 is characterized by a low tone relatively late in the stressed syllable, while accent 2 consists of a high tone early in the stressed syllable, falling to a low tone on the following syllable. The West Norwegian type ... is characterized by a high tone on the stressed syllable in accent 1, and a high tone on the following syllable in accent 2.
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tonal accent on the primary-stressed syllable in most Norwegian dialects; East Norwegian accent 1 = L*, accent 2 = H*L; West/North Norwegian accent 1 = H*, accent 2 = delayed H (L*H).

tone_statements.citation: Kristoffersen, Gjert (2006). Markedness in Urban East Norwegian tonal accent. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 29(1): 95-135. doi:10.1017/S0332586506001508. Open postprint: BORA hdl:1956/2401.
tone_statements.quote: A new formal analysis of the tonal accent contrast in Urban East Norwegian (UEN) is developed in this paper, based on Optimality Theory. Contrary to the widespread assumption that the contrast is based on privativity, this paper represents a return to the position that the contrast derives from different timing of a common underlying melody. Surface privativity, i.e. the absence vs. the presence of an H that can be observed in the contrast between accent 1 and 2 in UEN is analysed as the result of marked (accent 1) vs. unmarked (accent 2) association of a common tonal input.
tone_statements.summary: UEN binary tonal accent: accent 1 (lexically pre-linked, marked) vs accent 2 (default), same underlying melody with different alignment.

tone_statements.quote: Avhandlinga tek føre seg tonal fonologi, med hovudvekt på intonasjonsfonologi, men òg litt metrisk fonologi. Utgangspunktet for studien er sunnmørsk. TBU i sunnmørsk er mora. Den leksikalske tonen ved tonelag 2 er etablert som ein eigen morfo-leksikalsk tone (ulikt AP-grensetonen), ikkje som ein intonasjonell tone. Fokalitet i sunnmørsk vert markert gjennom ein ekstra låg tone og ny neddrift
tone_statements.translation: The thesis treats tonal phonology, with the main weight on intonational phonology, but also some metrical phonology. The point of departure is the Sunnmøre dialect. The TBU in Sunnmørsk is the mora. The lexical tone of tonal accent 2 is established as a separate morpho-lexical tone (unlike the AP boundary tone), not as an intonational tone. Focus in Sunnmørsk is marked by an extra low tone and renewed downdrift.
tone_statements.summary: West Norwegian (Sunnmøre) tonal accent: mora as TBU, accent 2 carries a lexical (morpho-lexical) tone distinct from the accent-phrase boundary tone; intonational L for focus, downdrift.

tone_statements.citation: Haugen, Einar (1967). On the rules of Norwegian tonality. Language 43(1): 185-202. doi:10.2307/411393. [Reprinted 1972 in E. S. Firchow et al. (eds), Studies by Einar Haugen, 531ff., Mouton, doi:10.1515/9783110879124.531.]
tone_statements.quote: A new analysis of the Norwegian (and Swedish) word tones is presented, according to which Accent I is regarded as the unmarked member and is identified with primary stress, while Accent II is regarded as the only distinctive tone. ... It is shown that tone is a feature of the post-tonic syllable, and that its presence in the native and much of the borrowed vocabulary is determined by the morphology; in other vocabulary items, the occurrence of tone is highly arbitrary, being lexically and dialectically determined, with virtually no minimal pairs possible.
tone_statements.summary: Privative word-tone analysis: Accent II = one distinctive (marked) tone located on the post-tonic syllable, Accent I = plain primary stress; distribution largely morphological.

sources.note: Describes Old Norwegian (13th-century medieval stage), not the modern language norw1258; the root-initial rule stated here is the Germanic native-vocabulary pattern. It is compatible with the catalog's existing statements, which already note that native (non-loan) Norwegian words have invariant initial stress (Lunden 2006; Rice 2006), while the catalog's weight-sensitive right-edge rule concerns modern loanword stress, which this thesis does not discuss. No contradiction; not a statement about the modern language.

sources.quote: The basic claim advanced in this talk is simple: Danish and E. Norwegian tones are completely predictable from prosodic and morphological context. Forms that are described as having 'stød' or 'Accent 1' have a low tone aligned to the right edge of a morphological (Danish) or prosodic (E. Norwegian) domain that is realized on the head syllable of a foot. ... Accent 1 invariably has a low trough toward the end of the stressed syllable, and Accent 2 invariably has a low trough toward the beginning of the post-stressed syllable.

sources.quote: As in Swedish, a tonal accent distinction is found in most Norwegian dialects. The distinction is dependent on primary stress, so that any primary stress will be pronounced with one of the two melodies that manifest the accent distinction. The phonetic manifestation of the melodies will vary with dialect, but two main groups can be identified. The East Norwegian type ... Here, accent 1 is characterized by a low tone relatively late in the stressed syllable, while accent 2 consists of a high tone early in the stressed syllable, falling to a low tone on the following syllable. The West Norwegian type ... is characterized by a high tone on the stressed syllable in accent 1, and a high tone on the following syllable in accent 2.
sources.note: Abstract (BORA/NVA record) states the system: tonal accent distinction in most Norwegian dialects, dependent on primary stress; East Norwegian type accent 1 = late L in stressed syllable, accent 2 = early H falling to L on next syllable; West/North Norwegian type accent 1 = H on stressed syllable, accent 2 = H on following syllable (plus posited L on stressed syllable). not downloaded: tone statement already listed here.

sources.quote: A new formal analysis of the tonal accent contrast in Urban East Norwegian (UEN) is developed in this paper, based on Optimality Theory. Contrary to the widespread assumption that the contrast is based on privativity, this paper represents a return to the position that the contrast derives from different timing of a common underlying melody. Surface privativity, i.e. the absence vs. the presence of an H that can be observed in the contrast between accent 1 and 2 in UEN is analysed as the result of marked (accent 1) vs. unmarked (accent 2) association of a common tonal input.
sources.note: OT analysis of the UEN accent 1/2 contrast as different timing of a common underlying melody; surface privativity (absence vs presence of H) derives from marked lexical pre-linking in accent 1 vs unmarked association in accent 2. not downloaded: tone statement already listed here.

tone.translation: The thesis treats tonal phonology, with the main weight on intonational phonology, but also some metrical phonology. The point of departure is the Sunnmøre dialect. The TBU in Sunnmørsk is the mora. The lexical tone of tonal accent 2 is established as a separate morpho-lexical tone (unlike the AP boundary tone), not as an intonational tone. Focus in Sunnmørsk is marked by an extra low tone and renewed downdrift.

sources.quote: A new analysis of the Norwegian (and Swedish) word tones is presented, according to which Accent I is regarded as the unmarked member and is identified with primary stress, while Accent II is regarded as the only distinctive tone. ... It is shown that tone is a feature of the post-tonic syllable, and that its presence in the native and much of the borrowed vocabulary is determined by the morphology; in other vocabulary items, the occurrence of tone is highly arbitrary, being lexically and dialectically determined, with virtually no minimal pairs possible.
